newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Donors set to rally around reforming Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Donors set to rally around reforming Vietnam.

text.p: Vietnam looks set for a major aid windfall of about $2.0 billion at an annual pledging session this week, a sure sign that Western governments remain determined to bolster the communist country's reform drive.

Diplomats said on Wednesday that donor nations and agencies, due to meet in Hanoi on Thursday and Friday, would send an unequivocal message of support to the government and back it up with aid commitments worth some $2.0 billion.
"Everyone likes a success story," the development cooperation counsellor of a European embassy in Hanoi said. "There's no donor fatigue here yet."

This year's aid will almost certainly add up to less than the $2.3 billion pledged at last year's meeting in Paris, which brought total commitments of official development assistance (ODA) since 1993 to $6.1 billion.
But the World Bank, which will chair the Consultative Group meeting, said $2.0 billion would still be a generous sum given that Western aid budgets are shrinking.
"If Vietnam can hold its own in a shrinking pie they're doing pretty well," said Bradley Babson, Resident Representative of the World Bank in Hanoi.
"People are still supporting the fundamental successes of Vietnam. You stand back and look at it, and they're doing pretty well," he told Reuters.

The World Bank, one of poverty-stricken Vietnam's top aid sources, has pencilled in $1.5 billion for development loans over the next three years to help upgrade the country's creaking infrastructure, welfare and education systems.
The donor community's enthusiasm is not entirely shared by many of the foreign investors who have flooded into Vietnam since doors to the outside world were opened 10 years ago.

Tired of waiting for problems of bureaucracy, rampant corruption, an opaque legal framework and high costs to go away, foreign firms have increasingly voiced their disappointment with Vietnam as an investment haven and many are looking elsewhere.

The Communist Party, at a landmark conclave earlier this year, agreed to pursue its cautious experiment in reform along market lines and set an annual economic growth target of 9-10 percent over the next five years.
However, there is still a conservative element pulling the other way, slowing progress in areas such as the development of a thriving private sector.
"Reforms need to be speeded up, and I'm sure ODA helps," said one European company executive in Hanoi.
"But frankly the donor community is so keen to see Vietnam do well that it only thinks in terms of carrots, not sticks."
Diplomats said red tape and a heavily centralised decision-making system were indeed to blame for the sometimes sluggish pace of aid disbursement in Vietnam.
Although about 27 percent of World Bank assistance has now been disbursed, other donors have paid out as little as one percent of their commitments.

The World Bank's Babson said disbursement was now set to pick up as long-planned infrastructure projects get under way and said donors would this week focus on aid quality rather than quantity to ensure help gets to the most needy areas quickly.
